## The AI Corner

**Priority: MEDIUM**

### Top Updates
* Yang Zhilin, founder of Kimi K2, shared his insights on why Claude's weak reasoning doesn't matter, why AGI has no finish line, and why running a company is reinforcement learning. He emphasized that Claude is not the best reasoner, but one of the best agents, and that reasoning and agentic ability come from two separate technical paths.
* Yang discussed the concept of the "brain in a tank" problem, where some AI products look smart in demos but collapse in production because they don't interact with the outside world. He also talked about the importance of token efficiency and optimizer research, and how these areas can lead to breakthroughs in AI development.
* The optimizer Muon was mentioned as a key component in achieving token efficiency, allowing models to learn from dependencies between parameters rather than treating each parameter independently. This approach can lead to significant improvements in model performance.
* Yang highlighted the importance of treating every solved problem as a new frontier, rather than a finish line, and emphasized the need for companies to rebuild their approach to innovation and problem-solving.
* He also discussed the concept of AGI as a direction rather than a specific step, and how it may not be a single moment or achievement, but rather a continuous process of improvement.
* The interview covered various other topics, including the role of reinforcement learning in managing teams, the importance of generalizing products beyond code execution, and the potential risks and benefits of AI development.

  - The master kill switch (cross-app tracking)
  - Killing Apple's ad profiling
  - Wiping the location diary
  - Locking down location app by app
  - Shutting off Siri's recording pipeline
- Apple settled a $95 million lawsuit in January after Siri was caught recording conversations through accidental activations and sharing them with contractors and advertisers, but even after fixing the issue, the ads continued because the microphone was never the main source of data collection.
- The 5 switches to kill the profile building include: 
  - Switch 1: Turning off "Allow Apps to Request to Track" (iPhone: Settings → Privacy & Security → Tracking) or "Delete advertising ID" (Android: Settings → Privacy → Ads)
  - Switch 2: Turning off "Personalized Ads" (Settings → Privacy & Security → Apple Advertising)
  - Switch 3: Turning off "Significant Locations" (iPhone: Settings → Privacy & Security → Location Services → System Services)
  - Switch 4: Setting location services to "Never" for apps that don't require location, and "While Using" for those that do
  - Switch 5: Turning off "Improve Siri & Dictation" (Settings → Apple Intelligence & Siri)
- These settings can be turned off in 2 minutes, effectively stopping the ads and making the phone's data collection less intrusive.

## Longevity.io Newsletter

**Priority: MEDIUM**

### Top Updates
* The FDA has approved a first-of-its-kind pill called enlicitide (sold as Lipfendra) for lowering stubborn cholesterol, offering a daily tablet alternative to recurring injections. The pill reduced cholesterol tied to artery buildup by 56% and 59% more than placebo in two randomized trials with 3,207 adults.
* Researchers discovered a connection between skin nerves and collagen, suggesting that preserving collagen may depend partly on keeping nerves and skin cells communicating with each other. A study found that removing nerves in mice sped up collagen loss, while restoring a nerve signal reversed some damage.
* A global analysis revealed that since 1990, life expectancy has increased by 9.2 years, while healthy life expectancy has only risen by 7.2 years, resulting in an average gap of 10.7 years worldwide and 14 years in the US.
* Brain scans found different aging patterns across nine brain disorders, indicating that future tools may need to show where the brain looks older, not just assign one age.
* A study on aging clocks found that five popular clocks tracked different genes and pathways in 3,227 adults, suggesting that one score should not be treated as a final verdict.
* Researchers identified tiny gateways and veins that help clear waste from around the brain, with the gateway route weakening with age in mice.
* Immune cells in old mice became worse at clearing spent immune cells, leading to increased inflammation across several organs. Restoring this function lowered inflammation, suggesting that failed cleanup may contribute to age-related inflammation.
* A federal pilot with Medicare will test whether real-world glucose-monitor data can guide approval and insurance decisions, potentially using information from devices people already wear.
* Hilo's $240 first-year system pairs a wrist tracker with a cleared arm cuff to show blood pressure trends between readings, although the wrist device is built for wellness, not diagnosing high blood pressure.
* FDA advisers are reviewing seven peptide-related ingredient families for possible use by compounding pharmacies, which may influence what pharmacies can offer in the future.

OpenAI has recently launched **Frontier**, an enterprise platform for building, deploying, and managing AI agents that can perform real work inside organizations’ existing systems.[1][2][3] Frontier lets companies create agents that connect to internal data sources and business applications, define granular permissions and governance, and run agents in a controlled execution environment, including support for agents built by third parties.[1][2][3][7] OpenAI positions Frontier as infrastructure for managing agents much like employees, with onboarding flows, shared business context, and feedback loops so agents can be evaluated and improved over time.[1][2][7]

This move matters because it shifts OpenAI deeper into the **enterprise AI/ML** stack, from providing general-purpose models to offering an orchestration and management layer for agent-based systems—an area where many large companies are currently struggling.[1][7][8] By targeting customers such as HP, Oracle, State Farm, Uber, and others, OpenAI is intensifying competition with rival platforms like Anthropic’s enterprise offerings and betting that managed AI agents will become a core component of business operations rather than experimental side projects.[1][4][5][7] In parallel, OpenAI is rolling out **workspace agents in ChatGPT** for Business, Enterprise, Edu, and Teachers plans—shared agents that teams can configure to handle complex workflows (coding, reporting, responding to messages) across tools like ChatGPT and Slack—further reinforcing an agent-centric product strategy that spans both enterprise platforms and day-to-day productivity use cases.[6]

AI Automation Society is a **global community and training platform** focused on helping people build and deploy real-world AI automations and automation agencies, even without a traditional coding background.[1] It is positioned as a resource-rich space for beginners, entrepreneurs, and operators who want to use tools like AI agents, APIs, Zapier, and no-code platforms to automate business workflows such as lead follow-up, appointment booking, and customer support.[1][2] The community is hosted on Skool and emphasizes practical implementation, process mapping, and systems thinking for AI-driven automation in small and mid-sized businesses.[1]

A key current offering is "AI Automation Society Plus," a structured program by Nate Herk that teaches the end-to-end process of launching an AI automation agency, including technical training, sales frameworks, templates, and ongoing support calls.[2] Recent content and reviews highlight its focus on helping members productize AI automations as a service (AIAAS), charge setup fees and recurring retainers, and stay current with rapid changes in AI tooling.[2] In the broader AI/ML space, AI Automation Society matters as part of a growing ecosystem of **applied AI communities** that translate frontier models into practical business automations, accelerating AI adoption among non-technical founders and operators and contributing to the rise of small, specialized AI agencies.

Cursor Router is an **intelligent model router** launched by Cursor for teams and enterprises that automatically selects the most appropriate LLM for each request based on task type, complexity, context, and domain.[1][3][6][8][9] Instead of developers manually choosing a single frontier model, Cursor Router uses a classifier trained on more than 600,000 live coding requests and evaluated across millions of production queries to route each request to either high-end frontier models or more price-efficient options while optimizing for user satisfaction and code “keep rate” (how much generated code remains in the codebase).[1][3][6][8][9] The system is integrated across Cursor’s desktop, web, iOS, CLI, and SDK and is available to Teams by default, with Enterprise administrators able to configure access, allowed models, and routing modes.[1][3][6][8]

It matters because it operationalizes **cost–quality tradeoffs** in AI-assisted development: online tests reported by Cursor show near–frontier-model performance at up to **60% lower cost**, with early enterprise users seeing 30–50% savings versus sending all work to a single premium model such as Opus 4.8.[3][5][6][8] Cursor Router exposes three modes—**Intelligence**, **Balance**, and **Cost**—that let organizations choose whether to prioritize maximum model capability, everyday quality at lower spend, or token efficiency while keeping output usable.[6][8] Industry commentary highlights that this moves model choice from manual “model loyalty” toward dynamic, per-request routing guided by empirical performance data, positioning routers as an important layer between coding agents and model providers in the broader AI/ML ecosystem.[6][7][8] As more teams adopt multi-model stacks and experiment with agents plus routers, Cursor Router is seen as both a practical cost-control tool for AI coding and a signal that intelligent routing will become standard infrastructure for production AI workloads.[6][7][8]

Anthropic is a San Francisco-based AI company best known for its Claude family of large language models and for positioning itself as an AI safety and research company focused on reliable, interpretable, and steerable systems.[3][8] Its latest public updates show rapid product and research momentum: Anthropic says Claude Code has become central to its own engineering workflow, and the company’s research page argues that AI is already accelerating AI development inside Anthropic, with Claude now authoring more than 80% of code merged into its codebase as of May 2026.[1] Anthropic’s newsroom also highlights recent product releases and coding-agent work, including Claude Opus 4.7 in April 2026 and a July 2026 piece on how Claude Code evolved from an internal tool into a coding agent.[6][7]

The most relevant recent industry context is controversy around Anthropic’s safety controls and its role in shaping frontier-model norms. In June 2026, reporting said Anthropic had hidden or softened model behavior when users appeared to be working on AI research, sparking criticism over transparency and competition concerns; Anthropic later said it was revising safeguards to make them clearer.[2][4] This matters because Anthropic is influencing both the technical direction of frontier AI and the policy expectations around model safety, especially as powerful coding and agentic systems become more capable and more central to enterprise and developer workflows.[1][2][8]
